questions.stem: What do the coronary arteries supply?

options.text: The cardiac muscle with oxygen and glucose
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Pulmonary vessels serve the lungs.
Brain supply runs via the carotid arteries.
Renal vessels serve the kidneys; urea is a waste, not a supply.

questions.stem: What mainly forms the fatty deposits in coronary heart disease?

options.explanation: Cells do not build the plaques.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Water hardness is not the named culprit.
Sugar is not the plaque material cited.

questions.stem: Which symptom follows PARTIAL blockage of a coronary artery?

options.explanation: Partial narrowing already causes pain on exertion.
Coughing is not the coronary symptom here.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
A heart attack needs complete blockage.

questions.stem: Why does complete blockage cause a heart attack?

options.text: Because the blood pressure falls to zero everywhere
options.explanation: The blockage is local, not systemic.

options.text: Because the plaque poisons the muscle
options.explanation: The damage is oxygen starvation, not poison.

options.text: Because the heart stops pumping entirely
options.explanation: Other regions may keep contracting; the starved region fails.

options.text: The muscle beyond receives no oxygen, so aerobic respiration stops and cells die
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: From which two sources does the body's cholesterol come?

options.text: Animal products in the diet and synthesis by the liver
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Neither is a cholesterol source.
Neither builds cholesterol.
Neither organ manufactures dietary cholesterol.

questions.modelAnswer: It is the build-up of fatty plaque inside the coronary arteries, restricting the flow that supplies cardiac muscle.

questions.stem: State what happens to the lumen as plaque builds up.
questions.modelAnswer: The lumen narrows and blood flow through the artery is reduced.

questions.stem: Explain why the heart muscle is especially vulnerable to blocked arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Because it contracts constantly and depends on aerobic respiration, so any interruption of its oxygen and glucose supply quickly starves the tissue it serves.

questions.stem: A patient reports chest pain only when climbing stairs. Suggest the coronary explanation.
questions.modelAnswer: Effort raises the muscle's oxygen demand, so a partially narrowed coronary artery cannot keep up, and the shortfall produces angina during exertion.

questions.stem: How does obesity raise coronary risk?

options.explanation: Thinning is not the mechanism; damage comes via diabetes and strain.

options.text: Extra weight strains the heart and can cause Type 2 diabetes, which damages vessels
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Obesity adds oxygen to the blood
options.explanation: It does not; it multiplies demand.
If anything, diet-linked cholesterol rises.

questions.stem: What does high blood pressure do to the vessels?

options.explanation: Pressure and rate are separate properties.
Pressure does not scour plaques.

options.text: The increased force against the walls damages them
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Damage narrows function rather than widening.

questions.stem: Which component of smoke reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells?

options.explanation: Nicotine drives plaque and pressure, not the oxygen grip.
Tar coats airways rather than red cells.
Exhaled gas is not the smoke component cited.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: How does smoking accelerate plaque build-up?

options.text: Chemicals in smoke increase both plaque growth and blood pressure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
It does the opposite.
Thinning is not the named effect.
The coronary link is explicit here.

questions.stem: Which risk factor speeds the deposits toward blockage most directly?

options.explanation: Sleep is not among the named four.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Pressure damages walls; cholesterol is the plaque material.
Obesity acts indirectly through strain and diabetes.

questions.stem: List the four risk factors named for coronary heart disease.
questions.modelAnswer: Obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking.

questions.stem: Name the diabetes type linked to increased weight in this context.
questions.modelAnswer: Type 2 diabetes can follow increased weight and further damages blood vessels.

questions.stem: Explain why several different risk factors end in the same disease.
questions.modelAnswer: Because each one pushes toward the same physical outcome — narrowed coronary arteries — whether through strain, wall damage, faster deposits or poorer oxygen carriage.

questions.stem: A smoker switches to a low-cholesterol diet. Which risk remains and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Smoking remains a risk, because its chemicals still raise blood pressure and plaque growth while carbon monoxide still cuts the oxygen carriage of the red cells.
